title: Grieving with others
hookLine: stay present when you don't know what to say
tomorrow: why did Peter refuse to let Jesus wash his feet?

cards: Bad news lands in the group chat: so sorry, a heart, then silence. When you don't know what to say, staying away can start to feel polite. Maybe they want space.
Maybe you'd only make it worse. In John's Gospel, Jesus reaches Bethany four days after his friend Lazarus has died. He already knows what he'll do; he's told his disciples he is going to wake him.
Then Mary, Lazarus's sister, falls at his feet weeping, and the people who came to comfort her are weeping too. And Jesus…

teach.b: "And Jesus wept." Three words in the Douay-Rheims, and they answer the puzzle. He isn't crying because he's lost hope; soon he'll call Lazarus out of the tomb.
John says that when he saw Mary weeping, and those with her weeping, he groaned in spirit and was troubled.

He wept because they were weeping. He didn't open with the plan or explain anything to a sister on the floor. He stood in the grief with them first, and the people watching said, behold how he loved him.
Paul makes it a habit in his letter to the Romans: "weep with them that weep." Not fix it, not explain it: weep with.
Its twin sits in the same verse, rejoice with them that rejoice: the same presence, in joy and in sorrow. Even the neighbors in this story know it.
John says people had come from Jerusalem to comfort the sisters, and their coming was the comfort. Catholics build this into the way they bury their dead.

Before the funeral there can be a vigil, where the community gathers with the family to pray and keep them company. So when you don't know what to say, the story's answer is that you may not need to. Bring yourself.

how: Catholics gather with a grieving family at a vigil for the deceased, at the funeral Mass and at the graveside, and the Church prays for the dead and comforts the mourning.

o: keeping your distance so they can grieve privately
staying present in someone's sorrow, words or not
helping a grieving friend find the bright side

games.q: grieving with others — tap the pairs.

s: Jesus wept because he had given up hope for Lazarus
he already meant to wake him. he wept because they were weeping.
people had come from Jerusalem to comfort Martha and Mary
John says so. their coming was the comfort.
the people watching said, behold how he loved him
his tears showed his love to everyone in the room.

games.q: a friend asks: if Jesus knew he'd raise Lazarus in a few minutes, weren't the tears just for show?
o: no: he wept because they were weeping, and he loved him.
yes: John added the tears to make the scene dramatic.
no: he wept because he doubted the miracle would work.
games.why: John says he groaned in spirit when he saw Mary and the others weeping, and the onlookers said: behold how he loved him.

practice: Close your eyes and bring to mind someone who is grieving right now, close to you or not. Don't plan what to say to them.
Just sit beside them in your mind for the whole stretch, the way you'd sit in a quiet room with nothing to fix. If you pray, you can hold their name before God; if not, simply hold it with care.

wordCard.voice: Grieving with others. Standing inside someone's sorrow with them, before any explanation, and sometimes without one. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: he shed tears. John 11:35, Jesus wept.

carryVoice: Keep this one: just stay, the way Jesus stood weeping before he said a word. Till tomorrow, then.
